strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel, naturalistic, human-annotated, document-level, cross-lingual benchmark for semantic difference recognition, addressing a real gap: most prior RSD work relies on synthetic, sentence-level augmentations.

Very comprehensive evaluation across a wide range of systems (unsupervised alignment baselines, few-shot and fine-tuned LLMs including reasoning models, and multiple encoder architectures) and three language pairs, with additional Kendall tau, inference-time, position-based, and cross-lingual label-projection analyses in the appendix.

Central empirical finding — a large and consistent performance gap between synthetic iSTS-RSD and naturalistic SwissGov-RSD across virtually all model types — is an important and practically relevant result for the MT evaluation/multilingual alignment community, cautioning against over-reliance on synthetic benchmarks.

High transparency: full annotation guidelines, interface screenshots, inter-annotator agreement statistics (including honest reporting of relatively low span-level agreement), and a dedicated analysis of how annotator discrepancies affect system rankings.

Useful qualitative and quantitative failure analyses (e.g., LLM output formatting failures, underlabeling near document ends, degradation with document length) that provide actionable insights for future work.
Data and code are released, and the paper contextualizes annotation agreement against related work (e.g., MQM error span annotation) to argue the agreement levels are within normal range.
weaknesses: Inter-annotator agreement at the span level is quite low (IoU 11–44%, F1 18–56%) with only two annotators per language pair, raising concerns about the reliability of the gold labels underlying the main results; the label distribution is highly skewed (only 10–17% of tokens annotated as differing), which could make Spearman correlation unstable despite the authors' attempt to mitigate this with Kendall tau.

No human/oracle upper-bound performance is reported to contextualize how much of the very low absolute scores on SwissGov-RSD (often single digits) reflects genuine task difficulty for models versus annotation noise or task ill-definedness.
The merging procedure for overlapping annotations (manual selection of 'better' annotations) introduces subjective curator bias that is not fully quantified.

Annotator pool is small (undergraduate students, not domain/translation experts) and language coverage is narrow (three closely related, high-resource, Latin-script languages paired with English), limiting generalizability of conclusions, as acknowledged in the Limitations section.

The comparison between iSTS-RSD and SwissGov-RSD conflates multiple confounds (domain, genre, document length, annotation protocol, naturalness) rather than isolating 'syntheticness' as the sole driver of the performance gap, weakening the causal interpretation of the central claim.

Some experimental choices (e.g., restricting LLM evaluation on SwissGov-RSD to only the best iSTS-RSD performers, per-model augmentation budget differences) reduce the comparability/completeness of certain result tables and are justified mainly by compute constraints.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: prior work on semantic difference recognition relied on synthetic, sentence-level benchmarks; this paper introduces the first human-annotated, naturalistic, document-level, cross-lingual dataset for the task (three EN-X pairs, 224 multi-parallel documents).

Extensive and carefully designed evaluation spanning unsupervised alignment baselines, few-shot LLM prompting, fine-tuned LLMs, and fine-tuned/pretrained encoder models of varying sizes and context lengths, giving a broad picture of the state of the art.

Annotation process is documented in detail (trial phase, guidelines, compensation, quality control via overlap-based IoU/F1/Spearman metrics, replacement of a low-quality annotator), and agreement statistics are transparently reported and contextualized against comparable tasks in the literature.

The central empirical finding — a large, consistent performance drop from synthetic iSTS-RSD to naturalistic SwissGov-RSD across virtually all systems and model classes — is a valuable and well-supported contribution that has clear implications for future benchmark design and model development.

Rich supplementary analyses (label-projection quality checks, document-length degradation analysis, inference-time comparisons, Kendall τ-b robustness check) strengthen the credibility and usefulness of the results.
Code, data, and detailed appendices (prompts, guidelines, domain breakdown) support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Inter-annotator agreement is fairly low (token-level Spearman 43.6–65.1), and for the majority of the dataset only a single annotator's labels are used (adjudication happens only for the 25 overlapping documents per language pair), which limits confidence in gold-label reliability and makes it harder to distinguish genuine model failure from annotation noise/task subjectivity.

The dataset is restricted to three closely related, high-resource, Latin-script languages within a single narrow domain (Swiss government web content), limiting the generalizability of the reported performance gap to other domains, language pairs, or scripts (acknowledged by the authors as a limitation).

The paper is primarily a benchmark/resource contribution rather than a new method; while the empirical analysis is thorough, the core novelty over related naturalistic comparable corpora (e.g., SwissAdmin, 20min-XD) is the token-level annotation layer rather than a fundamentally new resource type.

Dataset scale (224 document pairs per language pair) is modest for fine-tuning comparisons, and some evaluation choices (heuristic JSON repair, padding/truncating malformed LLM outputs, capping iSTS-RSD evaluation to 100 samples per setting) introduce additional noise that is not fully quantified.

The label-projection approach for non-English fine-tuning data relies on an LLM (GPT-4o-mini) whose quality is only spot-checked on 50 samples per pair, leaving open questions about systematic biases introduced into cross-lingual fine-tuning sets.

strengths: Introduces a novel, naturalistic, human-annotated, document-level, cross-lingual benchmark (SwissGov-RSD) for a task (RSD) that previously relied only on synthetic augmentations of sentence-level data, filling a genuine gap in the literature.

Very comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning unsupervised alignment baselines, multiple encoder architectures (including long-context multilingual encoders), open- and closed-source LLMs, few-shot prompting, reasoning models, and fine-tuning (LoRA for LLMs, regression heads for encoders), giving a broad picture of the state of the art.

The central finding -- a large, consistent performance drop from synthetic iSTS-RSD to naturalistic SwissGov-RSD across virtually all model families -- is a clear, well-supported, and practically important result for the MT-evaluation/multilingual-content community.

Careful and transparent annotation methodology: detailed guidelines, trial + main phases, multiple inter-annotator agreement metrics (IoU, F1, fuzzy/exact span correlation), explicit handling and disclosure of a problematic annotator, and an appendix analyzing how annotation discrepancies affect downstream conclusions.

Additional analyses (label projection quality check, inference-time comparison, performance vs. document length, Kendall vs. Spearman robustness check) go beyond the core results table and strengthen the reliability of the reported conclusions.
Data, code, and detailed prompts/appendices are provided, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Inter-annotator agreement is fairly low (token-level Spearman 43.6-65.1, with some subset correlations near zero or negative in Appendix A.4), raising concerns about the intrinsic reliability/ceiling of the task and complicating interpretation of low model scores as reflecting model failure rather than label noise.

The dataset is limited to three closely related, high-resource, Latin-script languages paired with English (explicitly acknowledged as a limitation), and covers only 224 government documents from a narrow set of domains (admin.ch subdomains), limiting generalizability claims.

Only two annotators per language pair with partial overlap (25 of ~110 docs) were used; discrepancies were resolved via manual inspection and merging by the authors, which could introduce subjective bias into the final 'gold' labels not fully captured by the reported agreement statistics.

The comparison between iSTS-RSD and SwissGov-RSD conflates several confounding factors simultaneously (domain, label distribution skew, naturalness, document length), so the attribution of the performance gap specifically to 'syntheticness' versus other distributional shifts is not cleanly isolated.

Due to computational constraints, several models (e.g., Llama-3.1 8B few-shot/fine-tuned, GPT-4o-mini few-shot, DeepSeek-R1, o3-mini) were not evaluated on SwissGov-RSD, weakening the completeness of the main comparison table for the paper's central claim.

Licensing constraints (source text remains copyrighted by Swiss authorities, only labels released) may complicate full reproducibility/reuse, since users must independently re-scrape and align the original documents.
